## Introduction

With a few edits to the hardware from [Lab 2](lab2.qmd), we can use the multiplexed display logic and row scanning on the keypad in order to reliably receive inputs from said keypad and display. Specifically, this lab aims to provide functionality to the keypad such that the display records the last two buttons hit on the keypad. In order to achieve this, a FSM reading inputs (to handle presses, lack of press, and multiple presses) was used in tandem with a register that would shift the last digit to the second display. Naturally, other modules in software are required to handle synchronization and debouncing on the keypad. This lab was an immensely thought provoking one and required a clever manipulation and communication between modules.

*I spent approximately 18 hours (so far) in this lab all together including familiarizing myself with the idea, debugging, and revising*

## Design and Testing Methodology

The overall logic was stored in four modules where the top module called on the counter, decoder, and scanner submodules. It also included the assign logic prescribing which digit to select (based on the count declared in the top module) and assigned LEDs to be the inverse of the column inputs in the scanner. On the topic of the scanner submodule, it contained a counter in it of itself (targetting that 2 Hz) and contained logic to scan a 4 x 4 keypad by setting a 4-bit row vector to exhibit HIGH across a bit, one at a time. As previously stated, the parameterized clock divider in the top module was 18 bits whereas here, it increased to 25 bits (lower frequency naturally).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Top Level Module Calls and Multiplexing Logic"}
    ```systemverilog
        logic int_osc;
    //Internal high-speed oscillator 48 MHz
        HSOSC hf_osc (.CLKHFPU (1'b1), .CLKHFEN (1'b1), .CLKHF(int_osc));

    //Leverage winker to get the desired Hz so they blink enough to not be seen
        logic [17:0] displayCount;
        winker #(18, ~18'b0) display(.int_osc (int_osc), .nreset (nreset), .en (1'b1), .count (displayCount));

        logic [3:0] sActive;
        assign sActive = ~displayCount[17] ? sRight : sLeft; //Multiplexer

        decoder decode(.s (sActive), .seg (seg)); //calls on decoder module 
        scanner scan(.int_osc (int_osc), .nreset (nreset), .en (1 me1), .row (row));

        assign digit[0] = ~displayCount[17];
        assign digit[1] = displayCount[17];
        assign led = ~col;
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Scanner Bit Shift Logic and Parameterization"}
    module scanner#(
    parameter WIDTH = 25,
    parameter MAX = ~25'b0)
    (
    input logic int_osc, nreset, en,
    output logic [3:0] row
    );
        logic [WIDTH-1:0] keypadCount;
        winker #(WIDTH, MAX) keypad(.int_osc (int_osc), .nreset (nreset), .en (en), .count (keypadCount));
        assign row = 1'b1 << (keypadCount[WIDTH-1:WIDTH-2]); //For the sake of parameterization

    endmodule
:::

For further elaboration, the scanner module was paramterized for the purpose of decreasing the clock division so an internally generated clock can properly exhibit the expected waveforms.

## Block Diagram

{#fig-block-diagram}
The block diagram in @fig-block-diagram demonstrates the overall architecture of the design. The top-level module lab2_ea includes three submodules: the winker/counter which is paramterized for displaying a range of frequencies to the top module or scanner (winker), the scanner which cycles between which bit of the [3:0] row output vector (fed into the keypad) is HIGH (scanner), and the 7-segment display logic module (decoder) Additionally, HS_OSC is also leveraged for an internal 48 MHz clock.Schematic{#fig-schematic}@fig-schematic shows the electical layout of the design. Because driving every segment at 10 mA is strenuous (especially if we consider a case where both digits display 8), 150 $\Omega$ was the appropriate value per the equation where $R_{seg} = (3.3V-2)/10mA$ making 150 our ideal choice. Additionally, the transistors and the resistor values associated with the keypad scanner were also paramount. First, to explain, the display was multiplexed by having 2 independent 2N3906 PNP transistors control a common anode of each digit respectively (specifically the Collector pin of the transistor). These transistors are configured such that they saturate when the FPGA pin (connected to Base) reads LOW. The Emitter is simply connected to +3.3V. Another thing to clarify is the NPN setup for each row of the keypad (4 row inputs). Following the E155 site instructions, the Emitter was grounded to the FPGA ground, the Base was connected to an FPGA pin (row outputs) via a resistor ($R_{base}$). The Collector was wired to the rows of the keypad as shown in @fig-schematic and the columns were wired both to the FPGA as column inputs and to +3.3V via a 1 k$\Omega$ pullup resistor. The value of this resistor is somewhat arbitrary and should be a decent value to pull-up. However, it does inform the value of $R_{base}$ as stated earlier. The equation is practically $R_{base} = (3.3V-0.7V)$ where 0.7V is the voltage drop across the resistor divided by $I_{base}$ which we expect to be $I_{collector}/10$ or 0.33mA. This ultimately yields a value of 7.8 k$\Omega$ though a 2.2 k$\Omega$ serves our purpose of saturating just fine.Results and DiscussionThe overall design and construction was successful as confirmed via simulation (incoming) and through the physical circuitry. I was able to accomplish all tasks outlined in the beginning of this lab report and utilize some interesting code and pin assignment workarounds. Overall, results are as expected and even with a few roadblocks in testbench logic (once again, incoming) and pins being assigned or not reading values.

    // Module 1: Common Anode Seven-Segment Decoder (4-bit BCD to 7-segment)// Common Anode logic: 0 = Segment ON, 1 = Segment OFF// Output mapping: {a, b, c, d, e, f, g}module seg7_decoder (input logic [3:0] bcd,output logic [6:0] seg);always_comb begincase (bcd)4'h0: seg = 7'b0000001; // 04'h1: seg = 7'b1001111; // 14'h2: seg = 7'b0010010; // 24'h3: seg = 7'b0000110; // 34'h4: seg = 7'b1001100; // 44'h5: seg = 7'b0100100; // 54'h6: seg = 7'b0100000; // 64'h7: seg = 7'b0001111; // 74'h8: seg = 7'b0000000; // 84'h9: seg = 7'b0000100; // 94'hA: seg = 7'b0001000; // A4'hB: seg = 7'b1100000; // b4'hC: seg = 7'b0110001; // C4'hD: seg = 7'b1000010; // d4'hE: seg = 7'b0110000; // E4'hF: seg = 7'b0111000; // Fdefault: seg = 7'b1111111; // Offendcaseendendmodule// Module 2: Time-Multiplexed Dual Seven-Segment Display Controllermodule seg7_mux_top (input logic clk, // System clockinput logic rst, // Active-high resetinput logic [3:0] in0, // First 4-bit BCD inputinput logic [3:0] in1, // Second 4-bit BCD inputoutput logic [6:0] seg_out, // Cathode segment drive outputs (shared)output logic [1:0] anodes // Common Anodes control (active-low));// Clock Divider / Multiplexing Toggle Flag
    // For hardware implementation, set counter size to refresh around ~1 kHz to prevent flicker
    logic [15:0] refresh_counter;
    logic        select_reg;

    always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin
        if (rst) begin
            refresh_counter <= '0;
            select_reg      <= 1'b0;
        end else begin
            refresh_counter <= refresh_counter + 1'b1;
            select_reg      <= refresh_counter[15]; // Toggles active display
        end
    end

    // 2-to-1 Multiplexer for BCD inputs
    logic [3:0] current_bcd;
    assign current_bcd = select_reg ? in1 : in0;

    // Single Decoder Instance
    seg7_decoder u_decoder (
        .bcd (current_bcd),
        .seg (seg_out)
    );

    // Active-Low Anode Controller (Enable one display at a time)
    // anodes[0] drives Display 0, anodes[1] drives Display 1
    assign anodes = select_reg ? 2'b10 : 2'b01;
    endmodule// Module 3: Testbenchmodule seg7_mux_tb;logic       clk;
    logic       rst;
    logic [3:0] in0;
    logic [3:0] in1;
    logic [6:0] seg_out;
    logic [1:0] anodes;

    // Instantiate Unit Under Test (UUT)
    seg7_mux_top uut (
        .clk     (clk),
        .rst     (rst),
        .in0     (in0),
        .in1     (in1),
        .seg_out (seg_out),
        .anodes  (anodes)
    );

    // Clock generation (100MHz)
    always #5 clk = ~clk;

    initial begin
        clk = 0;
        rst = 1;
        in0 = 4'h3; // Display 0 should show '3'
        in1 = 4'hA; // Display 1 should show 'A'

        #20 rst = 0;

        // Monitor multiplexing transitions
        #100000;
        $display("Input 0: %h, Input 1: %h", in0, in1);
        $finish;
    end
    endmodule
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Prompt with File Attachment"}
    module top_mux_7seg (input logic clk,input logic reset,input logic en,input logic [3:0] in0,input logic [3:0] in1,output logic [6:0] seg0,output logic [6:0] seg1);logic mux_sel;
    logic [3:0] current_in;
    logic [6:0] decoded_seg;

    // Instantiate provided clock divider/oscillator module
    blinker #(
        .WIDTH(23),
        .MAX(23'd10000) // Lowered max count to toggle faster for time multiplexing
    ) osc_inst (
        .int_osc(clk),
        .reset(reset),
        .en(en),
        .fpga_blink_out(mux_sel)
    );

    // Mux 1: Select between the two 4-bit inputs based on clock state
    assign current_in = mux_sel ? in1 : in0;

    // Instantiate provided 7-segment decoder
    decoder decoder_inst (
        .s(current_in),
        .seg(decoded_seg)
    );

    // Demux / Register output: Hold and display the decoded bits for each segment
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge reset) begin
        if (!reset) begin
            seg0 <= 7'b1111111; // Off state for common anode
            seg1 <= 7'b1111111;
        end else begin
            if (mux_sel) begin
                seg1 <= decoded_seg;
            end else begin
                seg0 <= decoded_seg;
            end
        end
    end
    endmodule
:::
